# Dissimilarity {#sec-dissimilarity}

## Background

There are multiple methods of describing palaeoecological data in terms of species communities. Older, but still valid, methods include CONISS [@grimm1987], which clusters samples into stratigraphic zones, amd more modern machine-learning methods, such as boosted regression trees [@elith2008; @simpson2012] and latent Dirichlet allocation [@blei2007; @blei2012]. Here, we are going to look at measures of dissimilarity between fossil assemblages such as the squared chord distance.  These sample-based dissimilarities provide the starting point for many kinds of paleoecological analyses.  In this chapter, we are going to look at how to build a distance matrix of community dissimilarity between every pair of samples in a core, then analyze the amount of change between temporally adjacent samples as a measure of community turnover over time.  In the next chapter, we will use dissimilarity analyses to identify fossil assemblages with no modern analogue. Although we will be using fairly simple implementations , dissimilarity/similarity is fundamental to many advanced methods in paleoecology and ecology.


::: {.callout-note}
# Packages required for this section

```{r dissimilarityPackages}
#| output: false
# Load up the package
if (!require("pacman")) install.packages("pacman", repos="http://cran.r-project.org")
pacman::p_load(tidyr, dplyr, ggplot2, scales, stringr, neotoma2, analogue)
```
:::


## Getting started

We will be using the Devil's Lake dataset downloaded in @sec-neotoma2, filtered for `datasettype == "pollen"`. We will read in the data from the data directory directly so that this section can be run independently of @sec-neotoma2. We've also included a catch-up block of code (below) that shows the process of downloading and filtering the data to maintain a reproducible record of the steps required to start this section.

::: {.callout-tip}
# Respawn code

This is the same Devil's Lake download used in @sec-age-depth, so if you have run that chapter the file is already on disk. The `datasettype` filter is important: site 666 carries five datasets, one of which is a modern **pollen surface sample**. Downloading without the filter appends that modern sample to the top of the core and it then behaves like the youngest level in that core, which is stratigraphically not quite correct.

```{r devilsDownload}
#| output: false
# Gated so the API is only contacted if the file is missing. Note the
# datasettype filter: site 666 carries five datasets, and one of them
# (3802) is a modern POLLEN SURFACE SAMPLE rather than part of the core.
# Downloading without this filter silently appends a modern sample to the
# top of a 14,000 year record.
if (!file.exists("./data/devils_dl.rds")) {
  devils_dl <- get_sites(siteid = 666) %>%
    get_datasets(all_data = TRUE) %>%
    neotoma2::filter(datasettype == "pollen") %>%
    get_downloads()
  saveRDS(devils_dl, "./data/devils_dl.rds")
} else {
  devils_dl <- readRDS("./data/devils_dl.rds")
}
```

:::

Recall from @sec-neotoma2 that `samples()` extracts the pollen counts from the download (along with lots of other useful variables!), and works offline because `get_downloads()` already fetched the data and we downloaded them to the data directory. The following code uses the `samples()` function to convert the downloaded data to a long table of each species recorded per sample and filters for upland herbs and trees and shrubs.


```{r devilsSamples}
devils_samples <- samples(devils_dl) %>%
  dplyr::filter(ecologicalgroup %in% c("UPHE", "TRSH"), # upland herbs, trees and shrubs
                elementtype == "pollen", # already done at the download stage, so not strictly necessary!
                units == "NISP")                        # counts, not percentages
```

### Harmonising and calculating proportions

Using the samples table, we can perform some simple programmatic harmonisation.
Neotoma records *Pinus* at Devil's Lake under three names: `Pinus undiff.`, `Pinus subg. Pinus` and `Pinus subg. Strobus`. To keep things simple we are going to aggregate all the *Pinus* species to genus level (e.g., lumping/aggregating all pines together) using `str_detect()` and `replace()`. Because the units are still counts at this point we sum the counts.

```{r devilsHarmonise}
devils_harm <- devils_samples %>%
  mutate(variablename = replace(variablename,
                                stringr::str_detect(variablename, "Pinus.*"),
                                "Pinus")) %>%
  group_by(siteid, sitename, sampleid, variablename, units,
           age, agetype, depth, datasetid, long, lat) %>%
  summarise(value = sum(value), .groups = "drop")

dplyr::n_distinct(devils_samples$variablename)
dplyr::n_distinct(devils_harm$variablename)
```

This aggregation is lumping together truly different subgroups of *Pinus* but is good enough for this demonstration. Now that we have done some simple harmonisation, we can convert the pollen count data to relative proportions. Typically (not always), pollen data are visualised in relative proportions, not counts or influx values, because count numbers are affected by interanalyst differences in total count, while Margaret Davis and co-workers showed that influx values were heavily influenced by within-basin variations in sediment focusing. Note that different statistical methods require different data forms (counts, proportions, scalar values, etc.), so be attentive to whether a given data form is compatible with a given statistical analyses. In this chapter we use proportions.

```{r devilsProportions}
devils_harm_prop <- devils_harm %>%
  group_by(age) %>%
  mutate(pollencount = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE),
         prop        = value / pollencount) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(desc(age))

# data check: every sample should sum to 1
range(tapply(devils_harm_prop$prop, devils_harm_prop$age, sum))
```

We save the harmonised proportions, because later chapters start from this object rather than rebuilding it. It is often a good idea to keep data on your own local computer (with a regular backup!) rather than relying on data persistence on a server.

```{r devilsSaveProp}
#| output: false
saveRDS(devils_harm_prop, "./data/devils_harm_prop.rds")
```

## From long to wide

The data are in long format as a [tibble](https://tibble.tidyverse.org/), which a modernized version of an R dataframe. This long format can be very convenient for data wrangling and plotting; however, many analyses require a specific input such as a wide (variables in columns) site-by-species matrix. It is important to be comfortable with pivoting data between long and wide formats and converting between dataframes/tibbles and matrices. Remember, that unlike dataframes and tibbles, matrices cannot be of mixed type (e.g., text strings and numbers).

::: {.callout-warning}
# Oh no! :scream:

Many statistical functions in R want a matrix, not a tibble or a dataframe (or other class), and `analogue::distance()` is one of them. Always check the package or function documentation (using `?`) for the required input format, because reshaping the data or changing its class may be necessary.

Functions should provide an error message if given the wrong input type; however, sometimes they will silently produce the incorrect result. For example, R will coerce numbers to characters if there is a single character column (like a naming column) in the matrix, and it does so without any error or warning. The coercion can go unnoticed when converting from a dataframe to a matrix, leaving you with a matrix that looks right and is the wrong type:

```{r stringMatrix}
string_matrix <- matrix(c("1", 2:10), nrow = 2) # see the numbers are in quotes indicating a string?
str(string_matrix) # Check the structure
```

Numeric matrix:

```{r numericMatrix}
numeric_matrix <- matrix(1:10, nrow = 2) # now the structure is int, for integer.
str(numeric_matrix) # Check the structure
```

Matrices can have row and column names (e.g., species names) and maintain a numeric structure, for example: `colnames(numeric_matrix) <- LETTERS[1:5]`. Check what you are about to pass in with `class()` and `str()`.
:::

The `analogue` package provides several distance measures that can be calculated for site-by-species matrices, we will use squared chord distance. So let's pivot our data to wide format and convert it to a numeric matrix. This can be done in several ways in R.  For consistency's sake we'll use `tidyr`:

```{r devilsPivot}
#| output: false
devils_samples_wide <- devils_harm_prop %>%
    tidyr::pivot_wider(id_cols = c(age, depth),
                       names_from = variablename,
                       values_from = prop,
                       values_fill = 0) %>% # Replace NA with 0 (see note below) 
    as.matrix()

# Some species were not recorded at certain depths (e.g., Acer at depth 603)
# one must be careful when replacing NA with 0 as 'not observed' is different to a measurement of 0
# in this case we can safely say that the proportion of Acer was 0 at a depth of 603 because
# Acer was found at other depths, so we know the analyst was looking for this pollen type.

devils_ad <- devils_samples_wide[ , c(1:2)] # store the ages and depths separately

devils_samples_wide <- devils_samples_wide[ , -c(1:2)] # drop ages and depth as they are not included in the distance calculations

```

## Calculating dissimilarity

Now we have our data in the correct format to do the distance calculation. Note that time is _not_ included as part of the calculation. The age and depth columns have been stored in a separate matrix `devils_ad`, and the squared chord distance will be calculated on the species community matrix `devils_samples_wide`.

```{r sqDist}
# Here we use method = "SQchord", see other available methods with ?distance
devils_sqdist <- analogue::distance(devils_samples_wide, method = "SQchord")
```

Print the first 5 rows and columns to see the structure:

```{r sqDistResult}
devils_sqdist[1:5, 1:5]
```

The `distance` function has returned a matrix of `r dim(devils_sqdist)[1]` x `r dim(devils_sqdist)[2]` dimensions. Note that the input dimensions were `r dim(devils_samples_wide)[1]` x `r dim(devils_samples_wide)[2]`. The function has calculated the distance between all pairwise samples, that is, every combination of 1 to $n$ samples. The diagonal of the matrix is each sample compared with itself and has values of zero. The upper and lower halves of the matrix mirror each other.

One way we can visualise these data is by picking an origin from which to compare change, and re-appending the time column (although, see the cautions below for this crude method). If we use the base of the core, the oldest sample, as our origin, we can look at how far the community moved away from that starting point as time runs forward to the present. The respawn code sorted the samples oldest first, so the oldest sample is the first row and column of `devils_sqdist`. Note that indexing by position like this only works if you know how your data are sorted. Let's bind that first column with our stored ages and depths, and plot distance over time.

```{r sqDistOrigin}
# Bind the age and depths variables with the first column of the SQdistances
origin_base <- cbind(devils_ad, sq_dist = devils_sqdist[ ,1])
```

```{r fig-dissimilarity-origin}
#| fig-cap: "Squared chord distance between each Devil's Lake sample and the oldest sample at the base of the core. The origin sits at zero on the left, and the rise towards the present shows the community moving progressively further from its initial composition."
origin_base %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = sq_dist)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_reverse(breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(6)) +
  labs(x = "Age (cal years BP)",
       y = "Squared chord distance from the base of the core") +
  theme_minimal()
```

We can see from @fig-dissimilarity-origin that the community at Devil's Lake changed substantially over the record, moving progressively further from the composition at the base of the core. Check out the pattern shown by applying the Modern Analogue Technique in @sec-novelty and how it compares to this plot.

However, plotting the distances with the original time column is not a formal time series analysis and does not take into account structural processes or autocorrelation. It's an exploratory method that it shows us patterns that may be of interest to investigate further.

::: {#exr-sample-to-sample}
@fig-dissimilarity-origin measures every sample against one fixed origin (the oldest sample). A different question is how much the community changed between one sample and the *next*.

Those values are already in `devils_sqdist`. The diagonal holds each sample compared with itself, so the comparisons between neighbouring samples sit immediately above (or below) it.

1. Extract the values one step off the diagonal (either above or below, not both) and plot them against age.  This plot represents the *magnitude* of community dissimilarity between adjacent samples, rather than the *rate*, because we haven't yet accounted for differences in time step between samples.

2. Compare your plot with @fig-dissimilarity-origin. Which parts of the record look like periods of rapid change, and would you have picked out the same intervals from the origin plot alone?

3. We might expect a longer gap between two samples to show a larger change, simply because more time has passed. Use `diff()` on the age column to get the gaps and check whether that is true here. Is the relationship what you expected, and what might explain it?

4. To calculate rates of change over time, divide each dissimilarity value that you calculated in step 1 by the time difference in step 3.  Plot rate of change against age.  How does the pattern for the rate-of-change time series differ from the magnitudes shown for plot 1?   

Be careful with the lengths. If you bind 122 values onto the 123 rows of `devils_ad`, R will not stop you: it recycles the shorter vector and gives you a full table with only a warning. That is worse than an error, because the plot still appears and one value in it is wrong. Check the lengths yourself before you bind anything.
:::

## Limitations of this method

Some considerations of this method are:

- time averaging is not taken into consideration. Time averaging is the amount of time a sample (i.e., a 1-centimetre thick slice of sediment core) encompasses. Due to processes like variable sedimentation rates and core compression, the number of years integrated within each sample may vary. Thus, we may be calculating the dissimilarity between say 50-years worth of ecological productivity and turnover in one sample, with 10-years in the previous one.
- the calculations are based on species composition alone and are not conditioned on environmental covariates (e.g., climate variables or fire). Thus, this method can be considered descriptive rather than inferential.

Squared chord distance is one of many measures of dissimilarity, and various papers have shown that it works well for pollen data [@overpeck1985; @gavin2003].  However, this metric is not necessarily the best for every pollen or other dataset [see @simpson2007]. The documentation of the `distance` function (accessed by `?distance`) lists the alternatives. The `vegan` package also includes functions for calculating distance, and provides many useful references in the documentation of the function `vegdist`.

::: {#exr-distance-metrics}
The choice of metric is a decision, not a default, and it changes the answer.

1. Use `?distance` to see the methods `analogue::distance()` accepts, then pick one other than `SQchord` and recalculate the distance matrix. Note that `chord` is closely related to squared chord distance, so choose something further afield, such as `euclidean`, if you want to see a real difference.

2. Plot your new distance-from-origin curve alongside the squared chord version. Check the range of each before you put them on the same axes: different metrics are not on a common scale, so a shared axis will make one look uniformly larger than the other for reasons that have nothing to do with ecology. Decide how to handle that, and justify what you did.

3. Do the two metrics agree about *when* the community changed, even where they disagree about how much? That is usually the more useful question of the two.
:::

::: {#exr-second-site}
So far we have been using Devil's Lake as an example, try calculate the squared chord distance:

1. Find another site in the upper Midwest (MN, WI, MI) with pollen data, either with `neotoma2` as in @sec-neotoma2 or through [Neotoma Explorer](https://apps.neotomadb.org/explorer/), and note its `siteid`.

2. Run the respawn code with your site in place of `666`. Expect to change more than the `siteid`. The code filters on the ecological groups `UPHE` and `TRSH`, on `elementtype == "pollen"` and on `units == "NISP"`, and it harmonises everything matching `Pinus.*` into a single taxon. Your record may not have all of those, and it will almost certainly need different harmonisation. Look at what you actually have before you filter, and keep a note of every decision you make on the way.

3. Build the distance matrix and rate of change for your site, and visually compare these to the curves that you built for Devil's Lake (the comparison will be easiest if everything is scaled to the same time axis).  What do you notice in terms of similarities or differences in pattern and timing?

4. Look at the pollen diagrams for these sites, either by building your own, looking at Neotoma Explorer, or going back to the original publications.  Assess which taxa are involved in the rate-of-change patterns at each site; how do they look the same or differ?

5. Go back to the age-depth homework and think about the age uncertainties for these two records.  How large are these age uncertainties, and, given this, what statements can be made with high or low confidence about the lead-lag relationships in the rate-of-change patterns between the two records? 
:::


## Conclusion

Despite the limitations of this method, it is a useful exploratory tool to visualise how the community composition has changed through time. In the Devil's Lake example, quite a stark change can be seen over the record, and this can provide a basis for further investigation.

The exercises take that further, and are worth returning to if you skipped them:

- @exr-sample-to-sample, change between neighbouring samples rather than from a fixed origin
- @exr-distance-metrics, and how much the choice of metric matters
- @exr-second-site, applying the whole workflow to a record of your own
